\title{\texorpdfstring{A rigid commensurate host and a defect that switches:\\
vacancies in the frustrated alternating spin-$(1,\tfrac12)$ Heisenberg chain}{A rigid commensurate host and a defect that switches: vacancies in the frustrated alternating spin-(1, 1/2) Heisenberg chain}}

\author{R.~L.~Silva}
\email{author@example.org}

\begin{abstract}
The alternating spin-$(1,\tfrac12)$ Heisenberg chain with a frustrating
next-nearest-neighbor coupling $J_2$ loses its Lieb--Mattis moment through a
discontinuous transition to a singlet whose nature was left open. Using an
SU(2)-symmetric density-matrix renormalization group, in which the total spin is
a quantum-number label, we identify that phase and follow a single vacancy
through it. The total spin collapses directly from $S=L/4$ to $S=0$, with no
partially polarized window. The singlet phase
is critical: its singlet--triplet gap closes as $1/L$, its entanglement entropy
grows logarithmically with a central charge $c\simeq1.8$, and its modulation
wavevector, extrapolated from $L=80$ to $200$, is commensurate at $3\pi/4$ and
independent of $J_2$ to $5\times10^{-5}$. Removing the central $S=1$ site
switches the ground state of the doped chain from a triplet to a singlet at
$J_2^{\ast}=0.3068(3)$, where the host shows no feature; the triplet is not
bound to the vacancy but spread over one of the two segments it leaves. The
transmission of correlations through the vacancy saturates at a finite value
below $J_2^{\ast}$, $T(\infty)=0.102(15)$ and $0.036(9)$ at $J_2=0.28$ and
$0.30$, and the cut-chain law $T\propto L^{-1}$ is excluded on both sides. We
also show that the longitudinal correlator is not an observable in a triplet
sector.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The alternating spin-$(1,\tfrac12)$ Heisenberg chain is the prototypical
one-dimensional quantum ferrimagnet. Its two inequivalent sublattices,
$S_A=1$ and $S_B=\tfrac12$, place the ground state in the total-spin sector
$S_g=(S_A-S_B)N_{\rm cell}=\tfrac12 N_{\rm cell}$ by the Lieb--Mattis
theorem~\cite{Lieb1962}, so the magnetization per unit cell is pinned at
$m=1/2$ and the spectrum carries a gapless ferromagnetic branch together with a
gapped antiferromagnetic one~\cite{Pati1997,Brehmer1997,Kolezhuk97}. An
antiferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor coupling $J_2$ frustrates each
sublattice against itself and eventually destroys this moment.

How the moment is destroyed was settled in outline by Ivanov, Richter and
Schollw\"ock~\cite{IvanovRichterSchollwock1998}. Zero-point fluctuations remove
the classical continuous commensurate--incommensurate instability, which for
$S_A/S_B=2$ would occur at $J_2/J_1=0.2$, and replace it by a discontinuous
transition to a singlet at a larger frustration; exact diagonalization of six
unit cells places it at $J_2/J_1\simeq0.229$. Inside the ferrimagnetic phase the
same work locates a disorder point at $J_2/J_1\simeq0.177$, beyond which
real-space correlations acquire an incommensurate component. What the singlet
state above the transition actually is was left open, and stated as such: the
nature of the $S_g=0$ ground states established beyond the ferrimagnetic phase
is named there as one of the important remaining questions. That is the question
we take up. The first-order character of the transition itself is not our
result; it is our starting point, and we reproduce it as a control.

The route to the singlet is not expected to be a single step. In frustrated
mixed-spin systems the generic scenario is an intermediate, partially polarized
ferrimagnetic phase between the Lieb--Mattis ferrimagnet and the nonmagnetic
state. Hida and Takano find such a phase in a mixed-spin chain with frustrated
side chains, carrying an incommensurate spin structure, and observe that this
structure is common to frustration-induced partially polarized ferrimagnets
generally~\cite{HidaTakano2008}. We find that the alternating chain does not
follow this route. With an SU(2)-symmetric density-matrix renormalization group
(DMRG), in which the total spin $S$ labels the sector rather than being inferred
from $\langle\mathbf S^2\rangle$, the ground state at $L=80$ is the Lieb--Mattis
value $S=20$ up to $J_2=0.22$ and $S=0$ from $J_2=0.24$ on. At these two
couplings we computed every sector from $S=0$ to $21$: between $S=0$ and the
Lieb--Mattis value the energy is monotonic in $S$, with its minimum at one end
of the range on one side of the transition and
at the other end on the other side, and what changes across the transition is
the tilt of the whole curve, not the appearance of an interior minimum. The
collapse is direct.

The singlet phase is critical --- its singlet--triplet gap closes as $1/L$ over
$L=80$ to $200$, and its entanglement entropy grows as $\ln L$ with a central
charge $c\simeq1.8$ --- and, within our resolution, rigid. Measured
through the SU(2)-invariant correlator
$\langle\mathbf S_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_j\rangle$ and extrapolated in $1/L$, the
modulation wavevector is commensurate, $q=3\pi/4$, and does not move with
$J_2$; at fixed $L$ it drifts monotonically, but the drift is a finite-size
correction whose amplitude shrinks with $J_2$ while the extrapolated value
stays put; the coupling at which that correction changes sign is itself a
finite-size quantity, moving from $0.3076(43)$ measured on $L=80,120$ to
$0.3263(18)$ on $L=120,160$ and back below $0.30$ on $L=160,200$, where the
correction is no longer resolved (Sec.~\ref{sec:pitch}).

That rigidity is what makes the defect problem sharp. A single impurity in a
one-dimensional interacting system is a singular perturbation: Kane and Fisher
showed that for $K<1$ an arbitrarily weak barrier grows under renormalization
until it cuts the chain~\cite{KaneFisher1992a,KaneFisher1992b}, while internal
degrees of freedom of the defect can open resonant channels and change that
fate~\cite{KaneFisher1992c,FurusakiNagaosa1994,EggertAffleck1992}. For a
single $S=1$ site removed from this chain, a preliminary study of ours with a
U(1)-symmetric code and the longitudinal correlator (unpublished; the U(1)
runs below) pointed to two behaviors: below a critical frustration, a vacancy
that binds a spin-1 moment and transmits correlations with a scale-invariant
plateau; above it, a vacancy that cuts the chain. We show here
(Sec.~\ref{sec:invariant}) that in the triplet sector the longitudinal
correlator depends on the magnetic quantum number $m$ of the member probed
and is therefore not an observable, so the transmission has to be rebuilt
from the invariant. Rebuilt (Sec.~\ref{sec:defect}), it separates the two
sides of a coupling $J_2^{\ast}$ by the sign of its finite-size correction:
below $J_2^{\ast}$ it saturates at a finite value, above it keeps falling,
and on neither side does it follow the cut-chain law.
The spin-1 moment, however, does not survive: below $J_2^{\ast}$ the doped
chain is a triplet, but the triplet is a magnon of the host confined to one
segment, not a moment bound to the vacancy, and $J_2^{\ast}$ itself depends on
where the vacancy sits.

The two transitions are, on the evidence assembled here, unrelated: the defect
changes its nature at $J_2^{\ast}$ while the host passes through that coupling
without a feature in its thermodynamic pitch. A defect transition in a rigid
commensurate host is the
central result of this work.

The system is not hypothetical. Bimetallic chains realize alternating
$(S,S')=(1,\tfrac12)$ Heisenberg ferrimagnets~\cite{Kahn1987,Hagiwara1998}, and
atom-by-atom assembly of mixed-spin structures has reached the point where such
chains can be built to specification~\cite{Huang25,Mishra21}, which makes the
tuning of $J_2$ a less remote prospect than it once was.

The paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:model} defines the model and
the vacancy convention. Section~\ref{sec:method} describes the SU(2) DMRG, its
validation, and the invariant observables. Section~\ref{sec:bulk} gives the
total-spin map and establishes the direct collapse. Section~\ref{sec:pitch}
settles the commensurability of the pitch. Section~\ref{sec:defect} presents
the vacancy, and Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses the separation of bulk
and defect physics.
\section{Model and lattice}
\label{sec:model}

We consider
\begin{equation}
H = J_1 \sum_{|i-j|=1} \mathbf{S}_i\cdot\mathbf{S}_j
  + J_2 \sum_{|i-j|=2} \mathbf{S}_i\cdot\mathbf{S}_j ,
\label{eq:H}
\end{equation}
on an open chain of $L$ sites, with $S=1$ on odd sites (sublattice $A$) and
$S=\tfrac12$ on even sites (sublattice $B$), so that $N_{\rm cell}=L/2$. Both
couplings are antiferromagnetic and $J_1=1$ sets the energy scale. The sums run
over pairs at distance one and two \emph{in the original site index}; this
phrasing is what makes the vacancy convention unambiguous.

\emph{Vacancy convention.} A vacancy is the removal of one site from the list of
sites, with Eq.~(\ref{eq:H}) still evaluated by the original distance rule.
Removing site $v$ leaves its two neighbors $v\pm1$ at original distance two, so
the $J_2$ bond between them survives: the hole is bridged by a single $J_2$
coupling, and both sublattices are preserved on either side. This is not a side
effect of bookkeeping; it is the physics of a missing magnetic ion in a chain
whose exchange paths are set by geometry. We use three lattices: \texttt{clean}
(all $L$ sites), \texttt{vacS1} (the central $S=1$ site removed; integer total
spin), and \texttt{vacS12} (the central $S=\tfrac12$ site removed; half-integer
total spin). Removal of the spin-$\tfrac12$ site dresses the defect with a
delocalized magnon and does not measure transmission through the defect; it is
kept as a control for the sector analysis only: with an $S=\tfrac12$ site
removed the chain has half-integer total spin and its correlations across the
defect are dominated by the $\pi$ component, so the incommensurate transmission
of Sec.~\ref{sec:estimators} is not a meaningful probe there and is not
reported.
\section{Method: SU(2) DMRG and invariant observables}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{SU(2)-symmetric DMRG}

Ground states are obtained with a two-site DMRG~\cite{White1992,Schollwock2011}
that exploits the full SU(2) symmetry~\cite{McCulloch2002,Singh2010},
implemented with the SU(2)-symmetric tensor libraries
\textsc{TensorKit} and \textsc{MPSKit}~\cite{TensorKit,MPSKit} in Julia. The
total spin $S$ of the state is a label of the symmetry sector in which the
sweep is carried out, not a quantity inferred afterwards from
$\langle\mathbf S^2\rangle$. Truncation is by a cap on the total bond dimension, counted as in a
U(1) or dense code (each SU(2) multiplet of spin $s$ contributes $2s+1$
states); we set it to $2400$, $3600$, $4800$ and $6000$ for $L=80$, $120$,
$160$ and $200$, scaling with $L$. The number of SU(2) multiplets actually
stored on the most entangled bond is about one quarter of that ($\simeq610$
and $\simeq910$ for $L=80$ and $120$, $\simeq1200$ for $L=160$,
$\simeq1500$ for $L=200$), which is the compression the symmetry buys. Sector
energies used to locate the ground state are converged to a
tolerance of $10^{-8}$ in $E_0$ with at most $100$ sweeps, sufficient to
separate sectors whose gaps are $\gtrsim10^{-3}$; the states used for
correlators are converged to $10^{-12}$ with at most $400$ sweeps. Six
states were converged to $10^{-10}$ with $200$ sweeps instead: three that
did not reach $10^{-12}$ within a wall-time cap (all within $0.002$ of a
level crossing, where the sweep stalls) --- the clean chain at $L=160$,
$J_2=0.31$, and the doped chains \texttt{vacS12} at $L=80$, $J_2=0.26$ and
\texttt{vacS1} at $L=120$, $J_2=0.30$ --- and, at $L=200$, the doped chain
\texttt{vacS1} at $J_2=0.28$ and $0.30$ (in the $S=1$ sector, whose sweep at
$10^{-12}$ had not converged after $19$ hours) and the clean chain at
$J_2=0.30$. On a state that converges either way, relaxing the tolerance
changes $E_0$ by $10^{-14}$, the pitch by $6\times10^{-10}$ and the
correlators by $4\times10^{-10}$; at $L=200$, $J_2=0.28$, the $10^{-10}$
ground-state energy agrees with the $10^{-8}$ sector probe to
$2\times10^{-11}$.

The singlet--triplet gaps of Sec.~\ref{sec:pitch} and the binding energies of
Sec.~\ref{sec:defect} use a second set of states, converged at bond dimension
$3600$ for $L\ge120$ ($2400$ at $L=80$), to $10^{-10}$ with at most $200$
sweeps, and then polished by five sweeps of a one-site DMRG with a tight local
eigensolver. The polishing addresses a limitation we found when validating
against exact diagonalization at $L=12$, where the bond dimension spans the
full space: the two-site sweep stops with an energy variance
$\langle H^2\rangle-\langle H\rangle^2\sim10^{-8}$, which costs $10^{-4}$ in
local observables, and the one-site sweeps bring it to $10^{-13}$. At $L\ge80$
the residual variance after polishing ($10^{-11}$ to $10^{-7}$) is set by
truncation instead. For one state, the clean chain at $L=200$, $J_2=0.28$,
$S=1$, the variance and the polishing step exceed the memory of the machine
used and were omitted; on the other $L=200$ states the polishing moved $E_0$
by at most $2\times10^{-8}$. Where states at the larger bond dimensions of the
previous paragraph also exist, the energies at $3600$ differ from them by at
most $3\times10^{-9}$ at $L=160$ and $6\times10^{-8}$ at $L=200$, five orders
of magnitude below the gaps.

\emph{Validation.} The engine reproduces exact diagonalization in 36 cases
($L=8,10,12$; the three lattices; four values of $J_2$) to $10^{-9}$ in $E_0$
and exactly in the total spin. The exact diagonalization is itself anchored to a
theorem: at $J_2=0$ the chain is bipartite with unequal sublattices and
Lieb--Mattis fixes $S=|S_A-S_B|$; the predicted values $2,\,2.5,\,3$
(\texttt{clean}), $1,\,1.5,\,2$ (\texttt{vacS1}) and $2.5,\,3,\,3.5$
(\texttt{vacS12}) for $L=8,10,12$ are reproduced in all nine cases.

\emph{Sector search.} Locating the ground-state sector by a local search around
the value found at the previous $J_2$ fails at a first-order transition, and
this failure is instructive: at $L=80$, $J_2=0.26$, such a search returns
$S=17$ with $E=-47.8575$ while $S=0$ has $E=-48.4046$, lower by $0.547$. The
ground state jumps from $S=L/4$ to $S=0$ without passing through the
intermediate sectors, so the low sectors must always be included in the
comparison. All maps reported below do so.

\subsection{The invariant correlator}
\label{sec:invariant}

We measure the SU(2) invariant $C(i,j)=\langle\mathbf S_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_j\rangle$
rather than the longitudinal $C^{zz}(i,j)=\langle S^z_iS^z_j\rangle$ used in
the U(1) runs. The difference is not one of normalization. Exact
diagonalization at $L=12$ shows that in a singlet the identity
$\langle\mathbf S_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_j\rangle=3\langle S^z_iS^z_j\rangle$ holds
to a residual of $4\times10^{-15}$, so for the clean chain in its singlet phase
the pitch and any ratio of correlators are unchanged by the substitution. In an
$S=1$ multiplet the identity fails by $0.3$--$0.76$, and $C^{zz}$ differs
between the $m=-1$ and $m=0$ members by up to $0.32$ while the invariant differs
by $7\times10^{-14}$. The longitudinal correlator in a triplet is therefore a
property of the member probed, not of the state, and the transmission through a
vacancy whose doped chain is a triplet has to be built from the invariant.

A second point follows from the symmetry. In an SU(2) eigenstate
$\langle\mathbf S_i\rangle=0$ identically, so there is no disconnected part to
subtract. Ferrimagnetic order, where present, appears as a non-decaying,
alternating $C(i,j)$, i.e.\ as weight at $k=\pi$; the incommensurate peak is a
separate feature, and the pitch search is restricted to a window that excludes
$\pi$.

\subsection{Estimators}
\label{sec:estimators}

\emph{Pitch.} For the clean chain we form the bulk-averaged correlator
$C(r)$ from pairs $(i,i+r)$ with $12$ reference sites $i$ in the central half
of the chain and $r\le0.45L$, and take the peak of its Hann-windowed Fourier
transform in $k\in[0.55\pi,0.95\pi]$, refined by three-point parabolic
interpolation. The estimator, windows and interpolation are identical to those
used with $C^{zz}$ in our U(1) runs, so that
the comparison with the U(1) numbers is one of identical estimator on a
different observable. The thermodynamic pitch is obtained by linear
extrapolation in $1/L$; the U(1) runs, with four or five sizes
($L=80$--$256$), showed the $1/L$ form to be preferred over $1/L^2$ by a
factor $11$--$25$ in residual.

\emph{Transmission.} The transmission of the modulated correlations across the
vacancy at $v$ is the ratio of Fourier amplitudes of the symmetric-pair
correlator $C(v-r,v+r)$, defect over clean, evaluated at the clean pitch
$q_{\rm IC}$ with a Hann window over $r/L\in[0.08,0.22]$ and $[0.10,0.25]$
(the spread sets the systematic error):
\begin{equation}
T_{\rm IC}(L)=\frac{|F_{\rm def}(q_{\rm IC})|}{|F_{\rm clean}(q_{\rm IC})|}.
\label{eq:T}
\end{equation}
The clean chain is sampled at the same center as the defect it normalizes,
which for \texttt{vacS1} is an odd site and for \texttt{vacS12} an even one.
Power counting at the cut-chain fixed point, to first order in the tunneling
between the half chains, gives $T_{\rm IC}\propto L^{1-2\eta}$, with $\eta$ the
decay exponent of the bulk spin correlator; the measured $\eta=1.0(1)$
(Sec.~\ref{sec:pitch}) makes this $T_{\rm IC}\propto L^{-1}$
(Appendix~\ref{app:scaling}). The criterion, fixed
before the larger sizes were run, is that pairwise slopes $b(L_1\!\to\!L_2)$
rise toward $1$ if the defect flows to
the cut chain, and stay near zero on a plateau.

Table~\ref{tab:Smap} gives the ground-state sector of the clean chain at
$L=80$. The Lieb--Mattis value $S=20$ persists up to $J_2=0.22$, and from
$J_2=0.24$ onward the ground state is the singlet. At these two couplings,
which bracket the transition, we did not rely on a local search: every sector
from $S=0$ to $21$ was computed. At $J_2=0.22$ the energy decreases
monotonically with $S$, from $-49.1655$ at $S=0$ to $-49.1685$ at $S=20$, in
steps of order $10^{-4}$; at $J_2=0.24$ it increases monotonically with $S$,
from $-48.5715$ at $S=0$ to $-48.4447$ at $S=20$, in steps of order $10^{-2}$.
The sector $S=21$, beyond the Lieb--Mattis value, lies more than one unit of
$J_1$ above the ground state at both couplings. Neither curve has an interior
minimum. What changes between the two couplings
is the tilt of the whole $E(S)$ curve, whose minimum jumps from one end of the
range to the other; a partially polarized phase would instead require an
interior minimum to develop, and none does. At couplings above $0.26$ the
competing sectors are higher in energy by at least the gaps listed, and at
$0.26$ the $S=17$ state found by a local search is $0.55$ above the singlet.
The collapse from $S=L/4$ to $S=0$ is direct, with no partially polarized
window of the kind that the frustrated mixed-spin scenario of
Ref.~\cite{HidaTakano2008} would predict.

Two remarks on what this table does and does not establish. First, the
transition is bracketed between $0.22$ and $0.24$; the finer value
$J_2^{c1}=0.233(3)$ from the $S^z$-resolved U(1) runs (Maxwell construction and
lever rule, Appendix~\ref{app:maxwell}) falls inside this bracket and is
consistent with the six-cell estimate $0.229$ of
Ref.~\cite{IvanovRichterSchollwock1998}. Second, the singlet just above a
first-order transition is a hard state for the DMRG: at $J_2=0.24$ the low
sectors took several hours each even at bond dimension 800. The sector
ordering, however, is decided by margins of $10^{-4}$ and more, far above any
truncation effect: between bond dimensions 800 and 2400 the $S=20$ energy at
$J_2=0.22$ moves by $6\times10^{-9}$ and the $S=0$ energy at $J_2=0.24$ by
$8\times10^{-6}$.

The gap column is the distance to the nearest sector, not the spin gap of the
singlet phase; it is included because it is the quantity the sector search
resolves, and it sets the tolerance a sector certification needs.

\emph{Agreement with the longitudinal estimator.} Where the clean chain is a
singlet the invariant and longitudinal estimators must agree, and they do:
at $L=80$ and $J_2=0.26,\,0.28,\,0.30,\,0.32$ the new pitch differs from the
$C^{zz}$ value by at most $6\times10^{-5}\pi$ (Table~\ref{tab:pitch}, last
column), a test of the engine rather than a new result.

\emph{Finite-size drift and extrapolation.} At fixed $L$ the pitch decreases
monotonically with $J_2$, from $0.7516\pi$ at $J_2=0.26$ to $0.7491\pi$ at
$0.35$ ($L=80$). The drift is a finite-size correction whose amplitude shrinks with
$J_2$, and whose sign depends on which pair of sizes measures it. Taking the
slope $b=\mathrm{d}q/\mathrm{d}(1/L)$ from the $L=80,120$ pair at every
coupling, so that one estimator is used throughout, $b=+0.033$ at $J_2=0.28$,
$+0.003$ at $0.305$, $-0.003$ at $0.31$, $-0.018$ at $0.32$ and $-0.086$ at
$0.35$: it passes through zero at
\begin{equation}
  J_2^{b=0}(80,120)=0.3076\pm0.0043 ,
  \label{eq:bzero}
\end{equation}
close to where the defect changes sector. The choice of Fourier window shifts
$q$ at the two sizes by the same amount and cancels in $b$; what does not
cancel is how much of the tail of $r$ enters the transform, and that sets the
uncertainty, $\pm0.004$ near the sign change, which is set by the per-point
error and not by the spacing in $J_2$.

\emph{The sign change is a property of the pair, not of the limit.} On the
$L=120,160$ pair, available at every coupling, the same estimator gives $b$
\emph{positive throughout} the window: $+0.055$ at $J_2=0.27$,
$+0.057$ at $0.28$, $+0.042$ at $0.30$, $+0.035$ at $0.3075$, $+0.032$ at
$0.31$, $+0.028$ at $0.3125$ and $+0.017$ at $0.32$, each with an uncertainty
of $\pm0.003$ from the same tail-of-$r$ systematic. This pair crosses zero
only between $0.32$ and $0.35$, at $J_2^{b=0}(120,160)=0.3263\pm0.0018$,
$9\sigma$ away from $J_2^{\ast}(L{=}80)$ and $0.019$ above the crossing of the smaller
pair; the coupling $0.26$, next to the first-order boundary, is the only one
where it is negative below $0.35$. The two pairs disagree about the sign of
the correction at every coupling between $0.3076$ and $0.32$, by ten times their common
uncertainty, so $q(L)$ does not follow a pure $1/L$ over these sizes. On the
largest pair, $L=160,200$, available at $J_2=0.28$, $0.30$ and $0.32$, the
pitch has stopped moving: $q(160)$ and $q(200)$ differ by $1$, $2$ and
$5\times10^{-5}$, at the level of the fit residuals, and the slope on that
pair ($+0.008$, $-0.016$, $-0.040$) is not resolved from zero at the first
two couplings. The coupling where the finite-size correction vanishes is
therefore itself a finite-size quantity that moves with the pair ---
$0.3076$ on $(80,120)$, $0.3263$ on $(120,160)$, below $0.30$ on
$(160,200)$ --- and the proximity of $J_2^{b=0}(80,120)$ to
$J_2^{\ast}(L{=}80)$ is a coincidence of one pair of sizes, not a relation
between two limits.

\emph{Two sizes are not enough.} How many sizes enter the fit matters at the
level of the effect we are after. Dropping $L=160$ and extrapolating from $L=80$
and $120$ alone raises
$q(\infty)/\pi$, for example by $0.6$, $1.2$ and $1.0\times10^{-4}$ at $J_2=0.28$, $0.305$
and $0.32$. The two-size estimator is biased upward by about
$10^{-4}$ --- the same size as the departure from $3/4$ it appears to resolve.
Every row of Table~\ref{tab:pitch} therefore uses at least three sizes; the
two-size values are drawn as open squares in
Fig.~\ref{fig:pitch}b, where the bias is visible as the offset between the two
symbols at each coupling.

\emph{The thermodynamic pitch does not move with $J_2$.} On five of the
couplings measured with the same estimator, $q(\infty)/\pi$ is $0.75003$,
$0.74990$, $0.74987$, $0.74988$ and $0.74994$ at $J_2=0.27$, $0.28$, $0.305$,
$0.31$ and $0.32$ (four sizes at $0.28$ and $0.32$, three elsewhere): equal
to $1.6\times10^{-4}$ over the whole interval and to $5\times10^{-5}$ over
$[0.28,0.32]$, where the three couplings with four sizes give $0.74990$,
$0.74989$ and $0.74994$ at $0.28$, $0.30$ and $0.32$, on both sides of the
defect transition $J_2^{\ast}$. The pitch of the host is thus rigid, and in
particular shows no feature where the ground-state sector of the doped chain
switches. What changes near $J_2\simeq0.31$ is only the direction from which
$q(L)$ approaches that limit on the $L=80,120$ pair, where
$J_2^{b=0}(80,120)=0.3076(43)$ sits $0.6\sigma$ from
$J_2^{\ast}(L{=}80)=0.3102$; on $L=120,160$ there is no sign change anywhere
in the window. Restricting the correlator sample to the interior of the
chain moves $J_2^{b=0}(80,120)$ between $0.306$ and $0.318$ without a trend,
and the defect crossing itself moves by $1.3\times10^{-3}$ between $L=80$
and $120$. The host registers $J_2^{\ast}$ in nothing that survives to the
thermodynamic limit.

\emph{What is not resolved.} Three sizes fit the linear form to an rms residual
of $\le2.3\times10^{-5}$, but that residual is not small compared with the
total variation of $q(L)$ over the same sizes, and the pair-dependence of $b$
above measures the same curvature more sharply: three points cannot separate
$1/L$ from $1/L+1/L^{2}$, and a quadratic through them is exact by
construction and returns $q(\infty)/\pi=0.7496$, $0.7494$ and $0.7495$. The
absolute offset of the thermodynamic pitch from $3/4$ is therefore not resolved
by the present data --- it is $0$, $-1\times10^{-4}$ or $-5\times10^{-4}$
according to the fit form. What is resolved, because one estimator is used
throughout, is that this offset does not depend on $J_2$. We take the
modulation to be commensurate at $3\pi/4$ and rigid. A fourth size at the
three couplings $0.28$, $0.30$ and $0.32$ narrows the linear-fit offset to
$-1.0$, $-1.1$ and $-0.6\times10^{-4}$ with residuals $\le2\times10^{-5}$,
but the change between $L=160$ and $200$ is of the same order as those
residuals, so the offset remains a bound; the four sizes fix the plateau and
its independence of $J_2$, which is what the conclusions rest on.

The residual at $J_2=0.26$ is the only resolved departure. With three sizes
the extrapolated pitch there is $q(\infty)/\pi=0.75137$, which is
$+1.4\times10^{-3}$ above $3/4$, with a fit
residual ($6.8\times10^{-5}$) three times larger than at the other couplings,
so that the $1/L$ form is already strained there. It lies next to the
first-order boundary $J_2^{c1}$; whether it is a genuine incommensurability
or the onset of the non-asymptotic regime seen at $L=40$ is not decided by the
present data.

\emph{Below $J_2=0.26$.} Immediately above the transition, at $J_2=0.24$
and $0.25$, the pitch is not reported: the ground-state sector at $0.24$ is
certified as the singlet (Table~\ref{tab:Smap}), but the pitch has not been
measured there with the SU(2) engine, and we do not quote pitches measured in
an inferred sector.

\emph{The singlet phase is gapless.} The rigidity of the pitch does not by
itself say whether the phase has a gap. We measured the singlet--triplet gap
of the clean chain, $\Delta_{\rm ST}=E_0(S{=}1)-E_0(S{=}0)$, at $J_2=0.28$
and $0.30$ on the four sizes (Table~\ref{tab:gapST}). At both couplings
$L\Delta_{\rm ST}$ is nearly constant --- $0.730$, $0.719$, $0.707$, $0.696$ at
$0.28$ and $1.189$, $1.215$, $1.229$, $1.237$ at $0.30$, for $L=80$ to $200$
--- and the extrapolation $\Delta_{\rm ST}=\Delta_\infty+b/L$ returns
$\Delta_\infty=-0.29\times10^{-3}$ and $+0.45\times10^{-3}$. Adding a $1/L^2$
term, or dropping $L=80$, keeps the intercepts within $0.3\times10^{-3}$ of
zero at $0.28$ and moves them to $+0.01\times10^{-3}$ and $+0.28\times10^{-3}$
at $0.30$. The gap therefore closes as $1/L$ to within a few times $10^{-4}$,
a twentieth of its value at $L=200$; the residual drift of $L\Delta_{\rm ST}$,
a few percent over a factor $2.5$ in $L$ and of opposite sign at the two
couplings, is what a marginal logarithmic correction would produce. This is
the direct evidence that the singlet phase is critical, which the pitch alone
does not supply.

\emph{Central charge and correlation exponent.} The entanglement entropy of the
clean chain identifies the critical theory more closely. For an open chain the
von Neumann entropy of the first $l$ sites follows
$S(l)=\frac{c}{6}\ln\big[\frac{2L}{\pi}\sin\frac{\pi l}{L}\big]+{\rm const}$
up to oscillating terms. We fit each residue class $l\bmod8$ separately over
$0.2L\le l\le0.8L$, which removes the period-eight oscillation, and average
the eight slopes, which scatter by $\pm0.2$--$0.3$ about their mean. At
$J_2=0.28$ and $0.30$ this gives $c=1.73$, $1.77$, $1.80$, $1.82$ and $1.72$,
$1.76$, $1.79$, $1.81$ for $L=80$ to $200$ (Table~\ref{tab:cc}); the entropy
averaged over one period at the center grows as $(c/6)\ln L$ across the four
sizes with $c=1.82$ at both couplings, and the windows $[0.1,0.9]L$ and
$[0.3,0.7]L$ move $c$ by less than $0.05$. The central charge is therefore
well above the value $c=1$ of a single SU(2)$_1$ chain and still drifts
slowly upward with $L$; these sizes place its limit between $1.8$ and $2$. The
spin correlations, by contrast, decay with the exponent of a single SU(2)$_1$
channel: the envelope of the bulk correlator $C(r)$, fitted class by class
($r\bmod8$) over $0.05L\le r\le0.35L$ against the chord distance
$\frac{2L}{\pi}\sin\frac{\pi r}{2L}$, gives $\eta=1.04$ at $J_2=0.28$ and
$0.99$ at $0.30$ for $L=200$; from $L=80$ to $200$ the value changes by at
most $0.02$, and by at most $0.04$ when the plain distance $r$ or the window
$[0.1,0.3]L$ is used. A spin
channel with $\eta=1$ alongside a central charge near $2$ points to a second
gapless mode that does not carry the leading spin correlation; identifying it
is beyond the scope of this work. For the transmission through a vacancy the
exponent that enters is $\eta$ (Appendix~\ref{app:scaling}).

\section{The vacancy}
\label{sec:defect}

\subsection{Ground-state sector of the doped chain and \texorpdfstring{$J_2^{\ast}$}{J2*}}

In a U(1) code the total spin of the doped chain can only be inferred, from
the splitting of the two lowest $S^z$ levels and from
$\langle\mathbf S^2\rangle$. Here
the sector is a label: for each $J_2$ we converge \texttt{vacS1} in $S=0$ and
$S=1$ (and \texttt{vacS12} in $S=\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac32$) and the ground
state is the lower of the two.
Table~\ref{tab:sectors} collects the two sector energies at $L=80$.

\emph{The ground-state sector of the doped chain switches at $J_2^{\ast}$.}
For \texttt{vacS1} the $S=1$ sector lies below $S=0$ at $J_2=0.26$, $0.28$ and
$0.30$, and above it at $0.32$; the splitting
$\Delta=E_0(S{=}1)-E_0(S{=}0)$ changes sign between $0.31$ and $0.315$
(Fig.~\ref{fig:gap}a). Linear interpolation on that bracketing pair puts the
crossing at
\begin{equation}
  J_2^{\ast}(L{=}80)=0.3102,
  \label{eq:jstar}
\end{equation}
and a quadratic through the three largest couplings returns the same value to
four digits. This is the same transition the $S^z$-resolved U(1) runs
placed at $0.312(2)$, now read off a symmetry label rather than from a
splitting of nearly degenerate $S^z$ levels: below $J_2^{\ast}$ the ground
state of the doped chain is a genuine spin-1 multiplet, above it a singlet.
The splitting is not monotonic --- it deepens from $-5.99\times10^{-3}$ at
$0.26$ to $-9.69\times10^{-3}$ at $0.28$ before rising through zero --- so a
linear form describes only the neighborhood of the crossing. Inside that
neighborhood it describes it well: the four couplings $0.30$, $0.31$, $0.315$
and $0.32$ lie on a straight line to within $3\times10^{-6}$,
$\Delta=0.326\,(J_2-J_2^{\ast})$, and the two couplings that bracket the
crossing most closely, $0.31$ and $0.315$, put it between them. Three
independent interpolations --- the pairs $(0.30,0.32)$, $(0.31,0.315)$ and
$(0.31,0.32)$ --- agree to $2\times10^{-5}$, so at this size
$J_2^{\ast}(L{=}80)=0.31019$ with a fit residual far below the last digit.

\emph{The crossing moves with size as $1/L$.} That number is a finite-size
quantity, and it is worth saying so plainly. Repeating the sector comparison
at $L=120$, bracketing couplings included, gives $J_2^{\ast}(L{=}120)=0.30886$,
lower by $1.3\times10^{-3}$; there too the three interpolations --- the pairs
$(0.30,0.32)$, $(0.31,0.315)$ and $(0.31,0.32)$ --- agree, to $1\times10^{-4}$,
and the four couplings lie on a line to $1\times10^{-5}$ with a slope $0.203$
against $0.326$ at $L=80$, the splitting itself shrinking with size. At
$L=160$ and $200$ the two sectors were converged at $J_2=0.28$, $0.30$ and
$0.32$, and the pair $(0.30,0.32)$, the one protocol available at every size,
gives $J_2^{\ast}(L)=0.31018$, $0.30890$, $0.30876$ and $0.30800$ at $L=80$,
$120$, $160$ and $200$.

The four values lie on a straight line in $1/L$,
$J_2^{\ast}(L)=J_2^{\ast}(\infty)+b/L$ with $b=0.27$, residuals within
$\pm3\times10^{-4}$, and extrapolate to
\begin{equation}
  J_2^{\ast}(\infty)=0.3068(3),
  \label{eq:jstarinf}
\end{equation}
where the uncertainty is the intercept's from the scatter of the four points;
a quadratic term in $1/L$ moves it by $10^{-4}$, and dropping any one size by
at most $3\times10^{-4}$; the first two sizes alone give $0.3063$. The small
step from $L=120$ to $160$ ($1.4\times10^{-4}$) is the largest residual of
the line ($+2.8\times10^{-4}$ at $L=160$), not a saturation of the drift.
The crossing is a property of the scaled spectrum. Near $J_2^{\ast}$ the
slope of the splitting, $0.326$ at $L=80$ and $0.203$ at $L=120$, falls as
$1/L$, so that $L\Delta$ crosses zero with a slope nearly independent of size
($26.1$ and $24.4$). Both levels approach the ground state as $L\to\infty$,
as they must in a critical host; what $J_2^{\ast}$ marks is a change in the
ordering of the lowest levels of the finite-size spectrum in units of $1/L$,
that is, in the boundary condition the vacancy imposes on the host.
What the drift does not touch is the
separation that this section is about: at every size the $S=1$ vacancy
crosses far from where the $S=\tfrac12$ control does, and the host has no
feature at either coupling.

\emph{The control transitions elsewhere.} Removing an $S=\tfrac12$ site
instead leaves a half-integer chain whose two lowest sectors cross at
$J_2\simeq0.262$ at $L=80$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:gap}b), far from $J_2^{\ast}$ and
close to the first-order boundary $J_2^{c1}$. Its size dependence is not a
drift but an alternation: at $L=160$ the two sectors are again degenerate at
$J_2=0.26$ (splitting $-3\times10^{-5}$, against $+4.4\times10^{-4}$ at
$0.28$), while at $L=120$ the splitting is already $+4.3\times10^{-3}$ at
$0.26$. The control crosses near $0.26$ when $L/8$ is even ($L=80$, $160$)
and not when it is odd ($L=120$), the same parity that modulates the
splitting of the $S=1$ vacancy below. The two defects therefore do not share a
transition: what happens at $0.3102$ is specific to removing the $S=1$ site,
not a property of doping the chain in general.

\emph{The triplet is not bound to the vacancy.} A spin-1 ground state does not
by itself mean that the vacancy binds a moment, and two measurements show that
it does not. The first is where the moment sits. The local moment
$\mu_i=\sum_j\langle\mathbf S_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf S_j\rangle/[S(S+1)]$, which
sums to one in the triplet, places $99.6$ to $99.8\%$ of it on one of the two
segments the vacancy leaves, at every size and at both $J_2=0.28$ and $0.30$,
spread along the whole segment with the period-eight modulation of the host.
The eight sites around the vacancy carry $0.30$, $0.22$, $0.17$ and $0.145$ of
it at $L=80$, $120$, $160$ and $200$ ($J_2=0.28$): the fraction falls as $1/L$
($L$ times it is $24$, $26$, $28$ and $29$) instead of saturating, as it would
for a bound state. At $L=80$ the profile is unchanged, to $6\times10^{-9}$,
when the sweep starts from a different random state, so the choice of segment
is not an accident of the algorithm. Which segment hosts the triplet
alternates with size --- the one to the right of the vacancy at $L=80$ and
$160$, the left one at $120$ and $200$ --- following the parity of $L/8$; the
triplet of the clean chain, for comparison, spreads over both halves. The
second measurement is the energy. A bound moment would keep the binding energy
$E_b=\Delta_{\rm ST}-\Delta$, the clean-chain gap of Table~\ref{tab:gapST}
minus the splitting of the doped chain at the same $J_2$ and $L$, finite as
$L\to\infty$. Instead $E_b\times10^{3}=18.8$, $11.8$, $9.2$ and $7.0$ at
$J_2=0.28$ and $18.2$, $11.9$, $9.1$ and $7.2$ at $0.30$, for $L=80$ to $200$:
$LE_b$ stays between $1.41$ and $1.51$, with the same parity alternation, and
its extrapolation in $1/L$ is within $1\times10^{-3}$ of zero for every fit
form we tried. Below $J_2^{\ast}$ the doped chain is a triplet of the critical
host confined to one segment, and $J_2^{\ast}$ is the coupling at which that
triplet crosses the singlet: a level crossing, not the ionization of a bound
moment. We keep calling $J_2<J_2^{\ast}$ the moment side, meaning the side on
which the doped chain carries $S=1$.

\emph{$J_2^{\ast}$ depends on where the vacancy sits.} Every size in this work
removes the site $v=L/2+1$. Moving the vacancy at $L=80$
(Table~\ref{tab:position}) shows that the crossing is tied to that choice.
When the segment to the left of the vacancy holds an even number of unit
cells ($v=21$, $41$, $61$), the doped chain behaves as described above --- a
triplet ground state below a crossing, the moment on one segment --- with
$J_2^{\ast}=0.3117$, $0.3102$ and $0.3088$; across positions the crossing
moves by $2.9\times10^{-3}$, more than its finite-size drift from $L=80$ to
$200$. When the left segment holds an odd number of cells ($v=11$, $31$, $51$,
$71$) there is no crossing in $[0.30,0.32]$: the ground state is a singlet
throughout, the triplet lies $2$--$3\times10^{-3}$ above it at $v=11$ and $51$
and only $4\times10^{-5}$ to $3\times10^{-4}$ above it at $v=31$ and $71$, and
its moment is shared equally by the two segments. The rule holds at all seven
positions, and we have no explanation for it; a test of the natural
candidate, a dimerization in pairs of cells, on clean chains with an odd
number of cells ($L=78$, $82$) found gaps of the same order as at $L=80$ and
rules it out. The rule survives at $L=160$: with the vacancy at $v=41$
($20$ cells to its left) the crossing is at $J_2^{\ast}=0.30809$ and the
moment sits on one segment, while at $v=51$ ($25$ cells) the singlet is the
ground state at both $0.30$ and $0.32$ and the triplet's moment is shared
equally. At $L=160$ the crossing for $v=41$ lies $6.7\times10^{-4}$ below the
one for the central vacancy, against a spread of $1.5$--$2.9\times10^{-3}$
among positions at $L=80$, so the dependence on position shrinks roughly as
$1/L$ (from two sizes, $L=80$ and $160$). All sizes used for
Eq.~(\ref{eq:jstarinf}) have an even left segment,
so the series $J_2^{\ast}(L)$ is homogeneous; $0.3068(3)$ is strictly the
limit for a vacancy at the center, but the shrinking spread suggests that the
limit does not depend on where an even-cell vacancy sits.

\emph{The bridge is what makes the crossing.} Removing the $J_2$ bond between
$v-1$ and $v+1$ as well as the site cuts the chain into two independent
segments, since the other bonds through $v$ go with it. Without the bridge
the splitting no longer crosses once: at $L=80$ it is $-18.2$, $+24.6$ and
$+3.2\times10^{-3}$ at $J_2=0.28$, $0.30$ and $0.32$, and at $L=120$ it
changes sign twice in the same window ($-5.9$, $+1.8$, $-2.2\times10^{-3}$),

\subsection{Transmission through the vacancy}

At $L=80$ the transmission of Eq.~(\ref{eq:T}), built from the invariant and
measured in the ground multiplet, falls steeply as $J_2$ approaches
$J_2^{\ast}$ from below: $T_{\rm IC}=0.340(20)$ at $J_2=0.26$, $0.082(8)$ at
$0.28$ and $0.018(5)$ at $0.30$; just above the transition, in the singlet
sector at $J_2=0.32$, it is back to $0.086(2)$. The vacancy is thus most
opaque at this size at the coupling just below the crossing.
